newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels, government inflexible on hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels, government inflexible on hostage crisis.

text.p: Despondency gripped Peru on Friday as neither President Alberto Fujimori nor the Marxist guerrillas holding 74 VIP hostages in Lima made any move toward resolving their 17-day-old standoff.

New Year's expectations of a prompt, peaceful solution to the siege disappeared as the realisation set in that the crisis would likely drag on for weeks -- unless Fujimori were to choose the military option.
"Unfortunately, that hope (for a negotiated end) has proved an illusion and the positions of both sides have hardened," Peruvian diplomat Antonio Belaunde wrote in an article.
Speculation that a deal could be cut to release some of the remaining hostages was quickly snuffed out by Japan.

"I would like to make it plain once again that neither Peru nor Japan have any intention of paying a ransom," Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto told a news conference in Tokyo on Friday.

Underlining the lack of progress in talks to resolve the crisis, the only activity at the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence on Friday was the usual shuttling to and fro of Red Cross workers, taking in food, medicines and, for the first time, books for the hostages.
They promised to send in "primitive" cleaning materials on Saturday to give the residence a much-needed cleanup.
There was no word from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels inside, and no sign of the government's negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo.

Following last week's first face-to-face meeting between Palermo and the guerrillas, Fujimori has kept his negotiator out of the building despite MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa's assurance that "the doors are open."
The rebels have not freed any hostages since Wednesday when seven were released following a visit by Juan Luis Cipriani, bishop of the Andean province of Ayacucho.
Cipriani, a close friend of Fujimori, has not been to the diplomatic compound since and the hostages remained caught between the uncompromising postures of the government and their captors.

While Fujimori has found replacements for government positions held by some of the hostages, the jungle-trained rebels said they could withstand the harsh conditions inside the residence even if their prisoners could not.

Without explanation, Fujimori removed from their posts on Thursday two police generals captured by the rebels -- the head of Peru's anti-terrorism force and the chief of national security. He also swore in a new Supreme Court president to replace Moises Pantoja, another hostage.

The security chiefs have come under fire for perceived security lapses that allowed the 20-odd MRTA rebels to storm a Dec. 17 cocktail party marking the 63rd birthday of Japanese Emperor Akihito and seized more than 500 VIP hostages.
Some commentators said Fujimori had made the removals to deliberately reduce the value of the hostages and to signal that the country's affairs went on despite the standoff.
The guerrillas also sent a message to the outside world, insisting that they could easily hold out "as long as it takes" but would not guarantee the same for the hostages.

"The guerrillas can stand it -- they've been trained in the jungle. But can the hostages?" MRTA spokesman Isaac Velazco said in an interview from Germany. "If they suffer, the Peruvian government must accept all responsibility for not facilitating a solution to this situation."
The remaining captives included Fujimori's brother, two ambassadors, top Peruvian government and security force officials, and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
The guerrillas were holding those men as bargaining chips to press their main demand for the release of roughly 400 comrades imprisoned in Peru.

That position was unlikely to have been assuaged by a speech by Fujimori on Thursday in which he condemned the rebels as "terrorists" bent on pointless violence. He also attacked the MRTA's claim to be fighting for the poor.

Fujimori's political position appeared more precarious on Friday after media reports that Peru's Constitutional Court had ruled as illegal a potential bid for a third term of office in 2000. Fujimori is widely believed to want a third term as president.
Officially, the court's magistrates said they had made a decision on Friday but would delay announcing it until the hostage crisis was over.

"We believe our decision is so important and delicate that it could cause political reactions that would not help this situation," Delia Revoredo, one of the Constitutional Court's seven magistrates, told reporters.

Opposition legislator Harold Forsyth proposed that former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, a diplomatic trouble-shooter and peace broker, step in to mediate the crisis. There was no immediate response from the government to his proposal.
